questions.prompt: A user program invokes a system call to read a file. Which sequence best describes the protection transition?
options: The wrapper places arguments, executes a trap/syscall instruction, and the CPU enters privileged kernel code
The process directly branches to the disk controller firmware in user mode
The CPU changes to kernel mode only after the disk returns data
The shell switches the process into kernel mode before every library call
answer: The wrapper places arguments, executes a trap/syscall instruction, and the CPU enters privileged kernel code
questions.explanation: The user-level wrapper prepares the ABI arguments; a controlled syscall instruction transfers execution to a kernel entry point with privilege checks.

questions.prompt: A C library function returns a cached value without entering the kernel. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a library/API call but not a system call on that execution
Every library function is necessarily a system call
It must still cause a mode switch because it is written in C
It is a hardware interrupt
answer: It is a library/API call but not a system call on that execution
questions.explanation: A library API may be implemented entirely in user space. Only operations that request kernel service need the syscall transition.

questions.prompt: A program calls printf to print a short string to a terminal. Which is generally true on a buffered stream?
options: printf may only update a user-space buffer; a later flush may invoke write
printf always maps to exactly one write system call
printf executes in kernel mode until the text is displayed
The terminal driver is called directly from the application
answer: printf may only update a user-space buffer; a later flush may invoke write
questions.explanation: Formatted I/O is a library operation. Buffering can combine or defer output, so the number and timing of write syscalls need not match printf calls.

questions.prompt: A process requests an operation requiring privileged access. Why does the ISA provide a syscall/trap mechanism?
options: It transfers control to a validated kernel entry while changing privilege in a controlled way
It lets user code set the processor privilege bit directly
It disables memory protection for the duration of the process
It lets the process choose any kernel instruction address
answer: It transfers control to a validated kernel entry while changing privilege in a controlled way
questions.explanation: The controlled entry mechanism prevents arbitrary user code from gaining kernel privilege or jumping into an unchecked kernel location.

questions.prompt: A system call blocks waiting for disk input. What normally happens to the caller while the device is working?
options: The kernel blocks it and schedules another ready thread or process
The caller continues executing the syscall instruction in a tight loop in user mode
The caller is terminated because disk I/O is asynchronous
The device interrupts the CPU continuously until completion
answer: The kernel blocks it and schedules another ready thread or process
questions.explanation: A blocking call changes the caller to a waiting state. The CPU can execute another ready context until an interrupt or completion event wakes it.

questions.prompt: A process performs a syscall and the operation completes immediately. Which transition is still required?
options: User mode to kernel mode and then return to user mode
No privilege transition occurs because no wait was needed
The process must be context-switched to a different process
The CPU must reboot into the boot loader
answer: User mode to kernel mode and then return to user mode
questions.explanation: Even a fast syscall enters privileged code; blocking and process context switches are separate possibilities, not mandatory parts of every syscall.

questions.prompt: Which event is asynchronous with respect to the instruction stream currently executing?
options: A device interrupt signaling completion of I/O
A system call instruction executed by the current process
A synchronous page fault caused by its load instruction
A breakpoint trap at its current instruction
answer: A device interrupt signaling completion of I/O
questions.explanation: A hardware interrupt can arrive independently of the current instruction. A syscall, page fault, or breakpoint is synchronous with execution.

questions.prompt: A user process executes an invalid opcode. Which description best fits the resulting exception?
options: It is a synchronous event caused by the current instruction and handled by the kernel
It is an asynchronous device interrupt
It is a voluntary system call that must return normally
It is an I/O completion notification
answer: It is a synchronous event caused by the current instruction and handled by the kernel
questions.explanation: An exception is tied to execution of a particular instruction; the kernel handles it according to architecture and OS policy, often by signaling the process.

questions.prompt: A syscall asks the kernel to copy 64 bytes from user memory. Why must the kernel validate the user pointer?
options: A malformed pointer must not let privileged code access arbitrary kernel or unmapped memory
User pointers are always physical addresses
The MMU cannot translate addresses during kernel execution
All user pointers become invalid immediately at a syscall
answer: A malformed pointer must not let privileged code access arbitrary kernel or unmapped memory
questions.explanation: Kernel code is privileged, so it must safely validate or use fault-tolerant copy routines when accessing user-controlled addresses.

questions.prompt: A syscall returns -1 and sets errno in a POSIX-style wrapper. What does this convention indicate?
options: The wrapper reports a kernel operation failure and exposes an error code
The CPU encountered a fatal hardware fault in every case
The process has necessarily been terminated
The kernel will automatically retry the call until success
answer: The wrapper reports a kernel operation failure and exposes an error code
questions.explanation: Many syscall interfaces return a failure sentinel and communicate a specific error through errno; failure does not imply process termination.

questions.prompt: A process requests creation of a new process. Which service category does fork-like functionality belong to?
options: Process control
File management
Device management only
Information maintenance only
answer: Process control
questions.explanation: Creating, terminating, and waiting for processes are process-control services, even if implementations differ across operating systems.

questions.prompt: A process invokes open on a pathname. Which service category is most directly requested?
options: File management
Process scheduling
Clock management
Memory compaction
answer: File management
questions.explanation: Opening a named file and obtaining a handle is a file-system service; later read/write operations use the returned descriptor or handle.

questions.prompt: Which pair is correctly classified as a communication-related system-call operation?
options: Creating a pipe and sending a message
Changing a process priority and setting a timer
Allocating a page table and mapping a file
Reading the system clock and obtaining process ID
answer: Creating a pipe and sending a message
questions.explanation: Pipes and message send/receive interfaces establish or use communication channels between execution contexts.

questions.prompt: A CPU runs user code, enters the kernel for a syscall, and returns to the same process without blocking. Has a process context switch necessarily occurred?
options: No; a privilege transition can return to the same process without scheduling another one
Yes; every syscall switches to a different process
Yes; entering kernel mode destroys the process context
No; syscalls execute outside both user and kernel contexts
answer: No; a privilege transition can return to the same process without scheduling another one
questions.explanation: Mode/privilege transitions change execution privilege; a process context switch changes which process or thread is scheduled. One does not imply the other.

questions.prompt: The kernel services a syscall, then a timer interrupt is pending and another process has higher scheduling priority. What may happen before the original caller resumes?
options: The scheduler may dispatch another process, so the caller resumes later
The syscall return address is discarded permanently
The interrupted process becomes a kernel thread
The timer interrupt converts the syscall into an exception
answer: The scheduler may dispatch another process, so the caller resumes later
questions.explanation: After handling the syscall and pending interrupt, scheduling policy may select another runnable context. The original process remains resumable.

questions.prompt: A syscall copies a structure from user space into a kernel buffer before using it. What security property does this primarily support?
options: Isolation from concurrent user changes and unsafe direct use of user-controlled memory
Guaranteed atomicity of all device operations
Elimination of the need for access checks
Prevention of all denial-of-service attacks
answer: Isolation from concurrent user changes and unsafe direct use of user-controlled memory
questions.explanation: Copying and validating user data into kernel-owned storage can avoid repeated access faults and some time-of-check/time-of-use hazards, though correct synchronization is still needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes a trap from an external interrupt in the usual OS terminology?
options: A trap is synchronous with the executing instruction; an external interrupt is asynchronous
A trap is always caused by a disk, while an interrupt is always caused by the timer
A trap is handled only in user mode
An interrupt cannot transfer control to the kernel
answer: A trap is synchronous with the executing instruction; an external interrupt is asynchronous
questions.explanation: A syscall trap or synchronous exception is caused by the current instruction; external interrupts originate independently, for example from devices or a timer.

questions.prompt: A process calls read(fd, buf, 1000), but a pipe currently contains 300 bytes and its writer remains open. Which result is generally permitted?
options: The call may return 300 bytes without filling the entire requested count
It must wait until exactly 1000 bytes are available
It must return 1000 bytes, padding the remainder with zeros
It must return an error because the request was partial
answer: The call may return 300 bytes without filling the entire requested count
questions.explanation: Many read interfaces permit short reads. Applications must inspect the returned byte count and loop when they require a fixed amount.

questions.prompt: A syscall accepts a file descriptor integer. Why is the integer not itself a kernel pointer?
options: It is an index/handle resolved through per-process kernel-managed descriptor state
It is a physical address encoded in decimal
The kernel dereferences it as user memory
It identifies a CPU register reserved for file data
answer: It is an index/handle resolved through per-process kernel-managed descriptor state
questions.explanation: A file descriptor is a small identifier into a process descriptor table; the kernel resolves it to an open-file object and associated state.

questions.prompt: A user program calls a system-call wrapper with an invalid syscall number. The safest kernel behavior is to
options: reject it with a defined error rather than dispatch arbitrary kernel code
treat it as a valid kernel function pointer
allow the user to select a privileged entry address
restart the CPU
answer: reject it with a defined error rather than dispatch arbitrary kernel code
questions.explanation: The syscall number must be checked against the supported interface; invalid numbers are rejected to preserve the kernel boundary.

questions.prompt: A workload makes 120 system calls. Each kernel entry/return costs 0.8 microseconds, excluding the service work. What is the total entry/return overhead in microseconds?
questions.explanation: Each call costs 0.8 microseconds for entry and return combined. Total overhead is 120*0.8=96 microseconds.

questions.prompt: A syscall wrapper incurs 0.4 microseconds on entry and 0.5 microseconds on return. For 200 calls, what is total transition overhead in microseconds?
questions.explanation: One call costs 0.4+0.5=0.9 microseconds. Across 200 calls the total is 180 microseconds.

questions.prompt: A program replaces 1000 separate one-byte writes with one 1000-byte write. If syscall transition overhead dominates and is constant per call, the change primarily reduces
options: The number of kernel crossings from 1000 to 1
The number of bytes delivered to the device
The TCP/IP headers per byte in every case
The need for the process to hold a file descriptor
answer: The number of kernel crossings from 1000 to 1
questions.explanation: Batching buffered output can reduce syscall frequency dramatically, though it does not necessarily change the amount of payload or lower-layer framing.

questions.prompt: A read syscall returns after copying data from a kernel page cache rather than waiting for storage. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The call still crosses into the kernel, but a physical-device wait may be avoided
No system call occurred because data was cached
The process must have performed DMA directly
The file descriptor is converted into a thread ID
answer: The call still crosses into the kernel, but a physical-device wait may be avoided
questions.explanation: A cache hit avoids a storage wait, not the syscall or privilege transition. Kernel-managed caches commonly satisfy reads without device I/O.

questions.prompt: Which actions typically require entering the kernel because they request protected operating-system services?
options: Create a process
Change a file descriptor table entry
Read a CPU register with an ordinary user-mode instruction
Request a blocking read from a device file
answer: Create a process
Change a file descriptor table entry
Request a blocking read from a device file
questions.explanation: Process creation, descriptor manipulation, and device reads request kernel-managed services. Ordinary user-accessible register reads may remain in user mode.

questions.prompt: A process executes a syscall that returns an error immediately. Which statement about CPU mode is correct?
options: The CPU still entered kernel mode to validate and reject the request
The kernel never ran because the result was an error
An error return implies a hardware interrupt occurred
The syscall is converted into a user-level function call
answer: The CPU still entered kernel mode to validate and reject the request
questions.explanation: Invalid arguments are normally checked by kernel code after entry; returning an error does not undo the privilege transition that already occurred.

questions.prompt: A hardware interrupt arrives while a process is in user mode. What does the CPU generally do before executing the interrupt handler?
options: Save sufficient execution state and transfer to a privileged interrupt entry
Ask the user process to call the handler as a normal function
Switch directly to another process without kernel code
Erase the interrupted process registers
answer: Save sufficient execution state and transfer to a privileged interrupt entry
questions.explanation: Interrupt entry preserves enough state to resume or schedule the interrupted context and transfers control to kernel code under privileged execution.

questions.prompt: Which event is most directly associated with a synchronous exception rather than an external interrupt?
options: A user instruction divides by zero
A network interface signals packet arrival
A periodic timer expires
A storage controller signals completion
answer: A user instruction divides by zero
questions.explanation: A divide-by-zero fault is caused by the instruction being executed, so it is synchronous. Device and timer events are asynchronous.

questions.prompt: A page fault occurs during a system call while the kernel copies from a user buffer. What must a robust kernel do?
options: Handle or safely report the fault without corrupting kernel state
Assume every user pointer remains mapped forever
Allow the faulting user instruction to overwrite kernel text
Disable address translation for the process
answer: Handle or safely report the fault without corrupting kernel state
questions.explanation: User memory can be unmapped or inaccessible even during a syscall. Kernel copy routines must handle faults safely and preserve kernel invariants.

questions.prompt: An application uses a library routine that internally calls getpid, which is implemented as a syscall on the target OS. How many kernel transitions does the library routine require?
options: At least one for the getpid syscall, unless the OS/library provides a user-space fast path
Exactly zero because the application called a library function
Exactly two syscalls for every library function
One transition per source-code line in the application
answer: At least one for the getpid syscall, unless the OS/library provides a user-space fast path
questions.explanation: The library wrapper itself is not necessarily a syscall, but if it invokes the kernel interface, that operation causes a controlled transition.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a system-call ABI is correct?
options: It defines conventions such as syscall numbers, argument locations and result/error handling
It defines only the visual format of shell commands
It is the same as a disk file system
It allows applications to depend on kernel internal data structures
answer: It defines conventions such as syscall numbers, argument locations and result/error handling
questions.explanation: An ABI specifies the low-level contract between user programs and the kernel, including how calls and arguments are represented and returned.

questions.prompt: Why can the same high-level library API have different syscall behavior on two operating systems?
options: The API may be implemented using different kernel interfaces or user-space mechanisms
System calls are fixed by the C language standard
All kernels use identical syscall numbers
The processor forbids OS-specific implementations
answer: The API may be implemented using different kernel interfaces or user-space mechanisms
questions.explanation: High-level APIs are portable abstractions; operating systems may provide distinct syscalls, combine operations, or satisfy some behavior in user space.

questions.prompt: A syscall transfers a 64-bit argument in two 32-bit registers on an ABI. What is the key requirement?
options: User and kernel sides must agree on register order and representation
The kernel may infer the argument from the process name
The application can choose arbitrary registers on each call without a convention
The OS must copy the argument to disk before entry
answer: User and kernel sides must agree on register order and representation
questions.explanation: The ABI fixes how multiword values are split and ordered; mismatched conventions would make the kernel interpret a different value.

questions.prompt: A syscall has a pointer and a length argument. What validation is most relevant before copying length bytes?
options: Check that the range is representable and safely accessible in the caller address space
Check only that the pointer is nonzero
Check that length equals the page size
Assume pointer+length cannot overflow
answer: Check that the range is representable and safely accessible in the caller address space
questions.explanation: A nonzero pointer may still be unmapped or invalid, and arithmetic on pointer plus length can overflow. Safe range validation/copying is required.

questions.prompt: Which can happen during a syscall that waits for a device?
options: The caller transitions to a waiting state
The scheduler runs another ready thread
A device interrupt later signals completion
The caller must busy-wait until the device is ready
answer: The caller transitions to a waiting state
The scheduler runs another ready thread
A device interrupt later signals completion
questions.explanation: Blocking I/O can deschedule the caller; device completion commonly arrives by interrupt and wakes it. Busy-waiting is not required for a blocking syscall.

questions.prompt: A syscall implementation copies a user string one byte at a time until it sees a null terminator. What risk must it handle?
options: The string may cross into an unmapped page before a terminator is found
A null terminator causes an automatic process switch
The kernel cannot read bytes from user space at all
Strings are always exactly one page long
answer: The string may cross into an unmapped page before a terminator is found
questions.explanation: User memory may end or become invalid at a page boundary. Kernel code must bound the scan and handle faults safely.

questions.prompt: A process invokes close on a descriptor. Which object is most directly removed from the per-process table?
options: The descriptor-table reference to an open-file description
The file?s disk blocks in every case
The process control block
The inode from all directories
answer: The descriptor-table reference to an open-file description
questions.explanation: Closing a descriptor releases that process-local handle/reference; the underlying open-file object and file data may remain reachable through other references.

questions.prompt: Two descriptors are created by duplicating one open descriptor. What may they share?
options: The same open-file description, including a shared file offset
Independent kernel processes
A single descriptor number in separate process tables only
The same user stack
answer: The same open-file description, including a shared file offset
questions.explanation: Duplicated descriptors can refer to the same open-file description, so file status and offset may be shared even though descriptor integers differ.

questions.prompt: A process calls lseek on one descriptor duplicated from another. What happens to the other descriptor if both refer to the same open-file description?
options: Its file offset changes as well
It is closed automatically
Its process is terminated
Its descriptor integer is rewritten
answer: Its file offset changes as well
questions.explanation: The offset belongs to the shared open-file description, not independently to each descriptor-table entry, so changing it through either affects the shared offset.

questions.prompt: A process calls exec-like functionality after fork. Which statement is generally correct?
options: The calling process image is replaced while its process identity is retained
A new process is always created by exec alone
The parent process is replaced
All open files are necessarily closed
answer: The calling process image is replaced while its process identity is retained
questions.explanation: Exec replaces the calling process address-space image with a new program; it does not by itself create a new process. Open descriptors may persist depending on close-on-exec flags.

questions.prompt: After fork-like process creation, both parent and child return from the call. Which value distinguishes their return paths?
options: The parent receives the child identifier; the child receives zero
Both receive zero
The parent receives zero; the child receives the parent identifier
Only the child returns from the call
answer: The parent receives the child identifier; the child receives zero
questions.explanation: The conventional fork interface returns different values in the two execution contexts so each can identify whether it is the parent or child.

questions.prompt: A process calls wait on a child that has already terminated but has not yet been reaped. What can wait do?
options: Return the child status immediately and reap its termination record
Block until the child is created again
Restart the child at its last instruction
Convert the child into a thread
answer: Return the child status immediately and reap its termination record
questions.explanation: A terminated child may remain as a zombie until its parent collects status. A wait call can return that status and release the process-table record.

questions.prompt: A parent exits while a child continues executing. Which general OS behavior applies?
options: The child can be reparented to a designated system process or supervisor
The child must always be killed at the same instant
The child becomes a kernel thread
The child loses its address space immediately
answer: The child can be reparented to a designated system process or supervisor
questions.explanation: Operating systems define reparenting/adoption behavior for orphaned children; parent termination alone does not universally require killing a live child.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a fork-then-exec process-launch pattern are correct?
options: fork creates a child execution context
exec replaces the calling process image
The child can close or redirect descriptors before exec
exec necessarily changes the process identifier
answer: fork creates a child execution context
exec replaces the calling process image
The child can close or redirect descriptors before exec
questions.explanation: Fork-like creation makes a child; exec replaces that child?s program image. Descriptor setup can occur first, and exec generally preserves the process identity.

questions.prompt: A syscall returns a file descriptor 0. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Zero is a valid descriptor value; success depends on the interface?s error convention
Zero always means failure for every syscall
The kernel returned a null pointer
The file has zero bytes
answer: Zero is a valid descriptor value; success depends on the interface?s error convention
questions.explanation: File descriptors are nonnegative small integers. Many Unix-like interfaces report errors with -1, making zero a valid success result.

questions.prompt: A syscall result is 0, but a separate output parameter contains a byte count. Which interpretation is safest?
options: Interpret the return value and output parameter according to that syscall?s documented contract
Assume zero always means no operation occurred
Assume the output parameter is ignored
Treat every output parameter as a kernel address
answer: Interpret the return value and output parameter according to that syscall?s documented contract
questions.explanation: System-call result conventions vary. The caller must use the defined contract rather than infer meaning from a value used by other calls.

questions.prompt: A device driver maps a user buffer for DMA. Why may the kernel pin or otherwise stabilize the pages?
options: The device must not DMA into physical pages that are freed or remapped during the transfer
DMA can access only filesystems
Pinning converts the buffer into a syscall number
The user process must become privileged
answer: The device must not DMA into physical pages that are freed or remapped during the transfer
questions.explanation: DMA occurs independently of CPU execution, so the OS may need to keep backing pages resident and correctly mapped until the device completes.

questions.prompt: A process invokes ioctl on a device descriptor. What does this typically represent?
options: A device- or driver-specific control operation
A standard operation to create a new process
A mandatory page replacement call
A DNS query made by the kernel
answer: A device- or driver-specific control operation
questions.explanation: ioctl is a generic interface for device-specific control requests where ordinary read/write operations are insufficient.

questions.prompt: Why should an OS expose a narrow system-call interface rather than all kernel functions directly?
options: It limits and validates privileged operations while preserving implementation flexibility
It prevents applications from using libraries
It guarantees no bugs can exist in the kernel
It makes every syscall execute in constant time
answer: It limits and validates privileged operations while preserving implementation flexibility
questions.explanation: A controlled ABI provides a security boundary and abstraction. It also lets the kernel change internal implementation without exposing internal functions.

questions.prompt: A syscall?s user argument points to a structure whose size differs across 32-bit and 64-bit ABIs. What design issue arises?
options: Structure layout and pointer-width compatibility must be defined or translated
The kernel cannot support either ABI
All fields automatically expand to 64 bits
The syscall number becomes the structure size
answer: Structure layout and pointer-width compatibility must be defined or translated
questions.explanation: ABI layout, alignment and pointer width affect how user structures are interpreted; compat layers may translate older layouts.

questions.prompt: A system call returns EINTR because a signal interrupted a blocking operation before completion. What should a robust caller consider?
options: Retrying may be appropriate, but it must follow the specific call?s partial-progress semantics
The kernel guarantees the operation completed fully
The process has necessarily received SIGKILL
The descriptor is permanently invalid
answer: Retrying may be appropriate, but it must follow the specific call?s partial-progress semantics
questions.explanation: Some interfaces can return partial progress or EINTR; callers should inspect the result and retry only according to that operation?s documented semantics.

questions.prompt: A blocking read is interrupted after transferring some bytes. Which outcome is possible on common POSIX-style interfaces?
options: It may return the number of bytes transferred rather than discard progress
It must always return -1 with no progress reported
It must restart from the original file offset without reporting bytes
It must terminate the process
answer: It may return the number of bytes transferred rather than discard progress
questions.explanation: Read may return a short positive count if some bytes were transferred before interruption. Applications need to account for partial completion.

questions.prompt: A syscall checks a pathname in user memory and later uses the same user pointer again. What class of bug could arise if the memory changes between checks?
options: Time-of-check to time-of-use inconsistency
Belady?s anomaly
Count-to-infinity
Priority inversion
answer: Time-of-check to time-of-use inconsistency
questions.explanation: User memory can be modified concurrently. Re-reading after validation may observe different data, so safe kernels copy or otherwise stabilize input where required.

questions.prompt: Which practices are appropriate when handling user pointers inside a kernel syscall?
options: Validate ranges and lengths for overflow
Use safe copy routines that handle page faults
Assume non-null means readable
Avoid trusting user-controlled structure fields without checking
answer: Validate ranges and lengths for overflow
Use safe copy routines that handle page faults
Avoid trusting user-controlled structure fields without checking
questions.explanation: A pointer can be non-null yet invalid, and lengths can overflow. Safe copies plus validation of fields maintain the privilege boundary.

questions.prompt: A user process passes a huge length that would overflow pointer-plus-length arithmetic. What should the kernel do?
options: Detect the overflow and reject the request before accessing the range
Wrap the address and continue copying
Disable address translation
Treat the length as a valid zero without checking
answer: Detect the overflow and reject the request before accessing the range
questions.explanation: Range computations must be checked for overflow; otherwise a malicious length can make an invalid range appear small or valid.

questions.prompt: A syscall copies a user-provided count into kernel memory, then iterates exactly that many records. What additional check is needed?
options: Check the count against interface limits and allocation-size overflow
Check only that the first record exists
Assume memory allocation cannot fail
Convert the count to a pointer without validation
answer: Check the count against interface limits and allocation-size overflow
questions.explanation: A bounded count prevents denial-of-service and allocation arithmetic overflow; each copied record still needs field validation as appropriate.

questions.prompt: A kernel syscall runs with interrupts disabled for a long time while scanning a user array. What is the main systems concern?
options: It can increase interrupt latency and harm system responsiveness
It improves fairness automatically
It makes user pointers inherently safe
It guarantees the scan cannot be preempted by hardware
answer: It can increase interrupt latency and harm system responsiveness
questions.explanation: Long interrupt-disabled regions delay servicing device and timer interrupts. Kernels keep such critical sections short and avoid unbounded user-controlled work there.

questions.prompt: A system call executes in kernel mode but on behalf of a user process. Which statement is correct?
options: The current process context can remain associated with the call even though execution is privileged
The kernel must create a separate process for every syscall
Kernel mode means the scheduler cannot run
The calling process address space disappears
answer: The current process context can remain associated with the call even though execution is privileged
questions.explanation: Syscalls commonly execute on the caller?s kernel stack/context while retaining its process identity and resources; blocking or preemption may later change the running context.

questions.prompt: A synchronous syscall is entered through a software instruction. What information must the kernel entry path obtain or preserve to return correctly?
options: The saved user execution state, including a return location and relevant registers
Only the current wall-clock time
The full contents of every disk block
The parent process?s source code
answer: The saved user execution state, including a return location and relevant registers
questions.explanation: The kernel must preserve enough architectural state to resume the caller with the defined result, including return address and registers per the ABI.

questions.prompt: A kernel validates a syscall number but not the requested operation?s arguments. Which security principle is still violated?
options: Complete mediation: each privileged operation must validate its relevant inputs
Least privilege is satisfied because the number was checked
The principle of locality
The end-to-end principle only
answer: Complete mediation: each privileged operation must validate its relevant inputs
questions.explanation: Checking the syscall number does not make untrusted pointers, sizes, flags or object permissions safe. Each request?s relevant inputs must be validated.

questions.prompt: A system-call instruction transfers control through a table of approved entry points. Which security benefit follows?
options: User code cannot select an arbitrary privileged instruction address as its entry
The kernel no longer needs argument validation
The process cannot be interrupted
The syscall executes without saving state
answer: User code cannot select an arbitrary privileged instruction address as its entry
questions.explanation: A constrained entry mechanism directs requests to vetted kernel handlers rather than allowing a user process to jump into arbitrary privileged code.

questions.prompt: A kernel switches from one process to another while returning from an interrupt. Which work distinguishes that from a simple syscall return to the same process?
options: Saving the outgoing schedulable context and restoring another context
Changing every user data byte
Recompiling the incoming program
Reinitializing the machine firmware
answer: Saving the outgoing schedulable context and restoring another context
questions.explanation: A process context switch preserves one execution context and restores another, often including address-space and register state; a same-process syscall return need not do that.

questions.prompt: A kernel uses a separate kernel stack for each thread. Why is this useful during a syscall?
options: It stores privileged call frames separately from the user stack
It removes the need for a process address space
It ensures every syscall is nonblocking
It stores only the syscall number permanently
answer: It stores privileged call frames separately from the user stack
questions.explanation: Separate stacks isolate kernel frames from user-controlled stack data and let the kernel safely resume a thread after privileged work.

questions.prompt: A vDSO-like user-space mapping provides a fast clock read. What is the intended advantage?
options: Some queries avoid a full syscall transition while using kernel-maintained time data
The process can modify the hardware clock directly
The clock read becomes an asynchronous interrupt
All time accuracy checks are removed
answer: Some queries avoid a full syscall transition while using kernel-maintained time data
questions.explanation: A vDSO can expose kernel-updated data and user-space code so common reads avoid entering the kernel, while kernel state remains authoritative.

questions.prompt: A syscall is interrupted by a signal before completion. Which behavior is possible depending on the call and signal policy?
options: The call may be restarted or may return an interruption error
All syscalls are always restarted transparently
The signal is ignored because the kernel is running
The process is always converted into a zombie
answer: The call may be restarted or may return an interruption error
questions.explanation: Restart semantics vary by syscall and signal configuration; callers must handle the documented return behavior.

questions.prompt: Which are examples of OS services commonly exposed through system calls?
options: Create or wait for a process
Open, read or write a file
Map memory into an address space
Change a local variable in user memory
answer: Create or wait for a process
Open, read or write a file
Map memory into an address space
questions.explanation: Process management, file operations and address-space mapping require kernel-managed resources. Updating a local variable normally stays in user mode.

questions.prompt: A user process attempts to write a kernel-only page. What mechanism normally prevents the write?
options: Hardware memory protection raises a fault before the write is allowed
The C compiler silently changes the page permissions
The kernel polls every user store
The file system rejects the instruction
answer: Hardware memory protection raises a fault before the write is allowed
questions.explanation: The MMU enforces page permissions on each access and raises a protection fault when user mode attempts a forbidden kernel-page write.

questions.prompt: A syscall returns before a device finishes a requested asynchronous transfer. What should the caller expect?
options: A separate completion mechanism is needed to learn when the transfer finishes
The return proves every byte reached the device
The device interrupt becomes the syscall return value automatically
The kernel must have terminated the process
answer: A separate completion mechanism is needed to learn when the transfer finishes
questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O separates submission from completion; callers need a completion event or status query before treating the operation as finished.

questions.prompt: A hardware interrupt arrives while a process is in user mode. What does the CPU generally do before executing the handler?
options: Save sufficient execution state and transfer to a privileged interrupt entry
Ask the process to call the handler as a normal function
Switch directly to another process without kernel code
Erase the interrupted process registers
answer: Save sufficient execution state and transfer to a privileged interrupt entry
questions.explanation: Interrupt entry preserves enough state to resume or schedule the interrupted context and transfers control to kernel code under privileged execution.

questions.prompt: A syscall returns EINTR because a signal interrupted a blocking operation. What should a robust caller consider?
options: Retrying may be appropriate, but it must follow the call?s partial-progress semantics
The kernel guarantees the operation completed fully
The process has necessarily received SIGKILL
The descriptor is permanently invalid
answer: Retrying may be appropriate, but it must follow the call?s partial-progress semantics
questions.explanation: Some interfaces can return partial progress or EINTR; callers should inspect the result and retry only according to the operation?s documented semantics.

questions.prompt: A kernel copies a user string until it finds a null terminator. What risk must it handle?
options: The string may cross into an unmapped page before the terminator is found
A null terminator causes an automatic process switch
The kernel cannot read user memory at all
Strings are always exactly one page long
answer: The string may cross into an unmapped page before the terminator is found
questions.explanation: User memory may end or become invalid at a page boundary. Kernel code must bound the scan and handle faults safely.

questions.prompt: A process changes its current working directory through a syscall. Is this normally global to all processes?
options: No; current working directory is normally process-specific state
Yes; every process immediately changes directories
Only the kernel can have a working directory
It changes the DNS search path only
answer: No; current working directory is normally process-specific state
questions.explanation: The working directory is normally maintained as part of a process context, so changing it affects that process.

questions.prompt: An interrupt handler acknowledges a device and schedules deferred work. Why defer part of the work?
options: Keep the immediate interrupt handler short so other interrupts are not delayed
Avoid ever entering kernel mode
Ensure the process runs before the device
Convert the interrupt into a syscall
answer: Keep the immediate interrupt handler short so other interrupts are not delayed
questions.explanation: Minimal immediate work reduces interrupt latency; longer processing can run later in a context where blocking or scheduling is permitted.

questions.prompt: A synchronous exception occurs at instruction address P. Which return choice depends on exception type?
options: Resume at P or at the following instruction according to whether the faulting instruction should be retried
Always resume at address zero
Always resume at the next process
Never return to the interrupted context
answer: Resume at P or at the following instruction according to whether the faulting instruction should be retried
questions.explanation: Faults may be retried after resolution, while traps may report completion and continue after the instruction; saved-PC semantics depend on the event.

questions.prompt: A process runs 10^6 user instructions and invokes a syscall every 1000 instructions. How many syscalls does it invoke?
questions.explanation: The call count is 10^6/10^3=10^3, or 1000 calls.

questions.prompt: Why can hardware privilege modes not replace syscall argument validation?
options: Privileged code can still be tricked into misusing invalid user-supplied values
The CPU cannot enter kernel mode
Arguments are encrypted by the MMU
User programs cannot pass pointers
answer: Privileged code can still be tricked into misusing invalid user-supplied values
questions.explanation: Privilege restricts direct user access, but kernel handlers execute with authority and must validate all user-controlled inputs.

questions.prompt: A syscall changes an open-file offset through a descriptor duplicated from another. What can happen to the other descriptor?
options: Its observed offset changes too if both refer to the same open-file description
It is closed automatically
Its process is terminated
Its descriptor integer is rewritten
answer: Its observed offset changes too if both refer to the same open-file description
questions.explanation: Duplicated descriptors can share one open-file description, including its offset, so seeking through either changes the shared offset.

questions.prompt: A system call checks a syscall number but ignores whether the caller may access the target file. Which property is missing?
options: Authorization of the requested object operation
Instruction decoding
Address alignment only
Interrupt prioritization
answer: Authorization of the requested object operation
questions.explanation: A valid syscall number does not grant access to every object; the kernel must still check credentials and permissions for the requested operation.

questions.prompt: A user process submits a very large buffer length. Which safety check is important before allocation or pointer arithmetic?
options: Check size limits and arithmetic overflow
Check only that the pointer is nonzero
Assume allocation cannot fail
Convert the count directly into a physical address
answer: Check size limits and arithmetic overflow
questions.explanation: A large length can overflow size computations or exhaust resources; validate bounds and handle allocation failure before accessing memory.

questions.prompt: A kernel ABI assigns stable syscall numbers. What does this stability primarily support?
options: Compatibility of user programs across kernel implementation changes
Identical execution time for every version
Unchanged internal function addresses
Automatic safety of all undocumented behavior
answer: Compatibility of user programs across kernel implementation changes
questions.explanation: A stable user-visible ABI lets binaries continue working as kernel internals evolve, provided documented semantics are preserved.

questions.prompt: Which operations normally require a protected kernel service rather than only ordinary user-mode computation?
options: Set a process scheduling priority
Create a file descriptor for a pathname
Add two local integers
Change a page mapping
answer: Set a process scheduling priority
Create a file descriptor for a pathname
Change a page mapping
questions.explanation: Scheduling priority, descriptor creation, and page mapping affect kernel-managed resources. Integer addition uses user-mode instructions.

questions.prompt: Which conditions can make a syscall block instead of returning immediately?
options: Requested pipe data is unavailable while a writer remains open
A device operation waits for completion
A file descriptor number is syntactically valid
A mutex-like kernel object is unavailable
answer: Requested pipe data is unavailable while a writer remains open
A device operation waits for completion
A mutex-like kernel object is unavailable
questions.explanation: A blocking read may await data, device operations may await completion, and synchronization calls may wait for a resource. A valid descriptor alone does not imply blocking.

questions.prompt: Which statements about syscall arguments are correct?
options: A pointer can be non-null yet invalid
A length can overflow range calculations
A kernel should trust user structure fields after copying them
A user buffer can become inaccessible during a copy
answer: A pointer can be non-null yet invalid
A length can overflow range calculations
A user buffer can become inaccessible during a copy
questions.explanation: Non-null pointers can be unmapped, lengths can overflow, and mappings can change. Copying alone does not make unvalidated fields trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A library implements gettimeofday-like behavior by reading a kernel-updated shared page in user mode. Which costs can be avoided on the fast path?
options: A syscall entry/return transition
All memory access costs
The need for kernel-maintained time state
All synchronization or consistency checks
answer: A syscall entry/return transition
questions.explanation: A user-space fast path may avoid privilege-transition overhead, but still reads shared memory and may need consistency checks against concurrent updates.

questions.prompt: A system call returns a positive number of bytes smaller than requested. What should the application generally do if it requires the full buffer?
options: Advance by the returned count and issue further reads as needed
Assume the remaining bytes are zero
Treat every short read as a kernel crash
Repeat the same call without advancing the buffer
answer: Advance by the returned count and issue further reads as needed
questions.explanation: The return count is progress. The caller should update the pointer and remaining length, and continue until the goal, EOF, or error.

questions.prompt: A process requests 4096 bytes in one read. The call returns 1536 bytes. How many bytes remain to be read to fill the requested amount?
questions.explanation: Requested bytes minus completed bytes is 4096-1536=2560. A follow-up read should begin after the 1536-byte prefix.

questions.prompt: A process issues close on a descriptor while another descriptor refers to the same open-file object. What is generally true?
options: Closing one descriptor need not destroy the shared open-file object
All aliases are closed unconditionally
The underlying file is deleted
The process terminates
answer: Closing one descriptor need not destroy the shared open-file object
questions.explanation: Kernel objects can remain alive while references exist. Closing removes one reference; other descriptors or processes may still use the open-file description.

questions.prompt: A kernel returns an error code from a syscall wrapper. Why is it unsafe for the application to assume no side effects occurred?
options: Some operations may make partial progress before reporting an error
Errors can only occur before kernel entry
The kernel rolls back every syscall atomically
An error return means the process did not run
answer: Some operations may make partial progress before reporting an error
questions.explanation: Calls such as read/write may transfer some bytes before an interruption or error. Their contracts specify whether partial effects are reported.

questions.prompt: A syscall performs a permission check and then blocks before using the resource. What concern can arise if permissions change while it waits?
options: The kernel may need to revalidate policy when the operation resumes or commits
The CPU forgets the syscall number
The process address space becomes a file
The syscall automatically becomes asynchronous
answer: The kernel may need to revalidate policy when the operation resumes or commits
questions.explanation: Long-running or blocking operations may need to recheck mutable authorization or object state before committing effects, depending on the security model.

questions.prompt: An OS uses a monolithic kernel. Which description is most accurate at this level?
options: Many core services execute in privileged kernel space, often in one kernel address space
Every service runs as a separate user process
System calls are unnecessary
Applications directly control devices
answer: Many core services execute in privileged kernel space, often in one kernel address space
questions.explanation: A monolithic kernel places many services such as file systems and drivers in kernel space; this can reduce IPC overhead but increases privileged-code size.

questions.prompt: A microkernel design moves many services to user-space servers. What trade-off is commonly involved?
options: More isolation/modularity may require additional IPC and context-switch overhead
It eliminates all message passing
It gives applications unrestricted device access
It makes system calls impossible
answer: More isolation/modularity may require additional IPC and context-switch overhead
questions.explanation: User-space servers can improve fault isolation and modularity, but service requests may require IPC and extra transitions compared with in-kernel calls.

questions.prompt: A hardware interrupt handler is executing with interrupts masked. Why should this interval be bounded?
options: Long masking delays other interrupts and increases response latency
It prevents any memory translation
It forces all processes to run
It guarantees device throughput increases
answer: Long masking delays other interrupts and increases response latency
questions.explanation: Masking interrupts protects short critical operations, but extended masking prevents timely timer/device handling and can harm responsiveness.

questions.prompt: A system-call entry uses a kernel stack and saves a return frame. What does the saved frame enable?
options: Restoring the caller?s execution state when the kernel returns or resumes it
Reconstructing the source code of the process
Recovering deleted file blocks
Choosing the domain name server
answer: Restoring the caller?s execution state when the kernel returns or resumes it
questions.explanation: The saved register and return state lets the kernel resume the correct user instruction stream with syscall results placed according to the ABI.

questions.prompt: A syscall handler verifies that a user pointer range is valid, then another thread in the same process unmaps it before copy-in completes. What must the copy mechanism handle?
options: A possible page fault or mapping change during the copy
The pointer automatically becomes a kernel pointer
The kernel may safely ignore the resulting fault
The other thread is necessarily killed
answer: A possible page fault or mapping change during the copy
questions.explanation: Address-space mappings can change concurrently. Robust copy routines handle faults and synchronize or otherwise define behavior for such races.

questions.prompt: A process invokes a system call while holding a user-space mutex. The syscall blocks. What risk can this create for other threads in that process?
options: They may be unable to progress if they need the held mutex
The kernel releases all user mutexes automatically
The mutex becomes a semaphore in the kernel
The process must be terminated
answer: They may be unable to progress if they need the held mutex
questions.explanation: A blocked thread retains user-level locks unless the application releases them; another thread needing that lock can stall, producing application-level deadlock.

questions.prompt: A process performs a syscall that returns quickly, then the scheduler runs a different process before the caller executes again. Which statement is correct?
options: The syscall itself need not have blocked; preemption can occur at a later scheduling point
A syscall return always guarantees immediate execution by its caller
The process must have been terminated
The scheduler cannot run after a syscall
answer: The syscall itself need not have blocked; preemption can occur at a later scheduling point
questions.explanation: Returning from the kernel makes the process runnable, but scheduling policy and interrupts may choose another ready context before it runs again.

questions.prompt: Which exception is most naturally handled by correcting state and retrying the same instruction?
options: A page fault for a valid page that was not resident
A breakpoint used to report completion after the instruction
A device interrupt
A process-exit syscall
answer: A page fault for a valid page that was not resident
questions.explanation: After the OS loads and maps the valid missing page, retrying the faulting memory instruction allows it to complete normally.

questions.prompt: A syscall table is indexed by a number in a register. What is the role of that number?
options: Select the requested kernel service handler from the supported interface
Identify the caller?s source-code line
Specify the physical address of the handler chosen by user code
Set the process priority automatically
answer: Select the requested kernel service handler from the supported interface
questions.explanation: The syscall number selects among defined services; the kernel validates it and dispatches to the corresponding implementation.

questions.prompt: A program invokes a function named read from a language runtime, which satisfies the request from an in-memory buffer. What is true?
options: That particular call may not enter the kernel at all
Every function named read must trap
The kernel must perform a disk transfer
The buffer is necessarily a page cache
answer: That particular call may not enter the kernel at all
questions.explanation: Names at the library/API layer do not guarantee a syscall. A runtime may fulfill buffered reads in user space and enter the kernel only when needed.

questions.prompt: A kernel changes an internal structure but keeps syscall behavior and ABI unchanged. What is the expected effect on a correctly written application?
options: It continues to work without knowing the internal change
It must read the new kernel structure directly
It must be recompiled for every internal refactoring
It gains kernel privilege
answer: It continues to work without knowing the internal change
questions.explanation: The syscall abstraction hides kernel internals. Applications depend on the documented interface, not private implementation structures.
